rows.title: The shift-additivity conjecture for periodic binary sequences
rows.record_statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer, let $c\geq \left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil$, and let $d=n-c$. Let $\mathcal{B}(n,c,d)$ denote the specified class of binary sequences, let $R^b(\mathbf{s}_n)$ denote the $b$-fold shift of $\mathbf{s}_n$, and let $\operatorname{add}(\mathbf{s}_n)$ denote its additivity parameter. Suppose that $0<b<n$ and that, for some $d_2$, $R^b(\mathbf{s}_n)\in\mathcal{B}(n,c,d_2)$ with $\operatorname{add}(R^b(\mathbf{s}_n))>\operatorname{add}(\mathbf{s}_n)$. **Shift-additivity conjecture.** Then $b=d_2$. The conjecture would extend the statements of the cited proposition and corollary from $c\geq\left\lceil\frac{2n-1}{3}\right\rceil$ to $c\geq\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil$, allowing the same conclusions about the unique relevant shift and the nonlinear complexity of the associated periodic sequence; the source reports experimental evidence but says that the proposed technique does not prove it.
rows.source: Qin Yuan, Chunlei Li and Xiangyong Zeng, “The structure and enumeration of periodic binary sequences with high nonlinear complexity”, arXiv:2602.01134 (2026).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds in its full range c ≥ ⌈n/2⌉. The source's Lemma 7 and Corollary 1 give b = d₂ when the two spacings and the two additivity parameters satisfy an inequality, which covers c ≥ ⌈(2n−1)/3⌉, and the authors say that their technique does not reach further. The new tool is a Run Lemma about the multiset of lengths of zero runs of the cyclic difference word of a sequence in the class B(n, c, d): comparing these run lengths before and after the shift handles the overlap that the published argument leaves open, and a reflection argument on cyclic windows finishes the proof. Lean states the source's Definitions 2 and 3 and the shift R^b literally for sequences Fin n → Bool, includes the membership of the original sequence in B(n, c, n − c) that the MathDB paraphrase leaves implicit, proves that the additivity parameter exists and is unique on the class, and proves the conjecture; it also shows by an example that the strict inequality in the hypothesis is needed.

rows.title: The uri multiplicity threshold shuffle conjecture
rows.record_statement:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of compositions, let $\ell(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ be the length of a composition, and let $\operatorname{ind}_a(\boldsymbol{\alpha})$ be its index at $a$. Define the uri multiplicities by

$$
\mu_{a,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=B_1(\ell(\boldsymbol{\alpha}),\operatorname{ind}_a(\boldsymbol{\alpha})),
$$

where

$$
B_1(m,n)=\frac{1}{m!}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{m}{k}B_k.
$$

**Uri multiplicity threshold shuffle conjecture.** The uri multiplicities satisfy the threshold shuffle identities from the source's definition. The supplied text gives no resolution status for these identities.
rows.source: Annika Burmester and Ulf Kühn, “On post-Lie structures for free Lie algebras”, arXiv:2504.19661 (2025).
rows.what_was_proved: The uri multiplicities satisfy threshold shuffle identity (i) of the source's Definition A.5 in full, and identity (ii) whenever the middle composition τ is nonempty; identity (ii) as printed, with no condition on τ, is false (at σ = τ = ∅, ϑ = (1), d₁ = d₂ = 0 it would assert 0 = −1). The corrected statement is what the source needs: the proof of its Theorem 5.11 uses (i) for adjacent factors and (ii) for factors separated by a nonempty word, its Example A.6(ii) follows that split, and the normalized solutions of its Remark A.8 are incompatible with the printed empty case. The proof expands the multiplicities over the cuts of a word, uses the compatibility of shuffle with deconcatenation and a divided-difference identity for the Bernoulli-type numbers B₁(m, n), and cancels the remaining alternating sum over cuts of the middle word, which is where τ ≠ ∅ enters. Lean states Definition A.5 and the multiplicities literally (with multiplicity 0 at non-positive thresholds, which implements the omission of inadmissible insertions), proves (i), proves (ii) for τ ≠ ∅, proves the counterexample to the printed (ii), and reproduces both parts of the source's Example A.6.

rows.title: Conjectural interval-family homomorphisms from dihedral type to type A
rows.record_statement:
Let $1\le b\le a<n-1$ and $a>1$. For the type-$A$ braid monoid, write $w_0^{[r,s]}$ for the longest element of the parabolic subgroup on the interval $[r,s]$.

**Interval-family homomorphism conjecture.** The assignments

$$
\widehat{T}_1\mapsto T_{w_0^{[1,a]}},\qquad \widehat{T}_2\mapsto T_{w_0^{[b,n-1]}}
$$

define a homomorphism $\operatorname{Br}^+(I_2(N))\to\operatorname{Br}^+_n$ if one of the following holds:

$$
N=\frac{2n}{n+b-a-2}\in2\mathbb Z_{>0};
$$

$$
a+b=n\quad\text{and}\quad N=\frac{n}{b-1}\in1+2\mathbb Z_{>0};
$$

$$
a+1=2(b-1),\quad a+b<n,\quad\text{and}\quad N=6.
$$

The paper presents these as a conjectural infinite family of non-disjoint standard homomorphisms and reports verification for $n\le15$.
rows.source: Arkady Berenstein, Jacob Greenstein and Jian-Rong Li, “Artin monoids, their homomorphisms and twins”, arXiv:2606.26776 (2026).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds in all three cases and for every n: the two half twists (positive lifts of the longest elements on the intervals [1,a] and [b,n−1]) satisfy the braid relation of length N in the positive braid monoid, so they define a monoid homomorphism from the dihedral Artin monoid Br⁺(I₂(N)). Cases I and II follow from a periodic-braid identity: rotation and overlap identities for half twists, proved by positive rewriting. Case III (N = 6) comes from a seven-move identity on four strands, transported to all sizes by cabling with strands of unequal width. The source proves the subfamilies N = 3 (of case II) and N = 4, b ≥ 2 (of case I) and reports computer verification for n ≤ 15. Lean works in the presented positive monoid on σ₁, …, σ_{n−1} with the braid and commutation relations, defines the half twists as explicit triangular positive words, and proves both the alternating relation and the existence of the homomorphism with no premise beyond the conjecture's hypotheses; an earlier group-level proof is kept.

rows.title: The affine type B distance conjecture
rows.record_statement:
Let $w$ be an affine signed permutation in $\widetilde{S}^B_n$. An integer $j\in[n-1]$ is **good** if $w$ restricts to a bijection from $\pm[j]$ to itself, and it is **very good** if this restriction is an even-signed permutation. Define

$$
\operatorname{bl}^{\widetilde{C}}(w)=1+\#\{\text{good values for }w\},\qquad \operatorname{bl}^{\widetilde{B}}(w)=1+\#\{\text{very good values for }w\}.
$$

Here $\$(w)$ and $\operatorname{dis}(w)$ denote the quantities defined for affine signed permutations in the paper. **The affine type B conjecture.** If $w\in\widetilde{S}^B_n$, then

$$
\$(w)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{dis}(w)+\operatorname{bl}^{\widetilde{C}}(w)-\operatorname{bl}^{\widetilde{B}}(w).
$$

This conjecture extends the finite-type formula to affine type $\widetilde{B}$. If true, it would imply $\$(w)-\operatorname{dis}(w)/2\leq n$ for all $w\in\widetilde{S}^B_n$; the corresponding boundedness behavior is contrasted with the affine type $\widetilde{D}$ case.
rows.source: Joel Brewster Lewis and Bridget Eileen Tenner, “Bargain hunting in a Coxeter group”, arXiv:2302.04404 (2023).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds for every n: the cheapest way to write an affine signed permutation w of type B as a product of reflections of that group, where a reflection costs its depth, costs dis(w)/2 + bl_C(w) − bl_B(w). Lower bound: every reflection changes the displacement by at most twice its cost, and a crossing-count lemma shows that each good cut that is not very good (an odd block) forces one extra unit of cost, because a product of reflections of the type B group restricted to a block that is preserved by all of them has an even number of sign changes. Upper bound: a greedy rule that always applies an efficient swap, and switches the partner of the swap whenever the obvious choice would close an odd block, reaches the identity at exactly that cost; its termination and invariants are proved. The source proves the analogous formulas where no branching occurs and in finite type D; in affine type B no depth formula was available. Lean defines the group as permutations of the integers with the periodicity, negation and parity conditions, takes costs over lists of reflections each of which belongs to the group, and proves that the doubled formula dis(w) + 2(bl_C(w) − bl_B(w)) is the least element of the set of doubled costs, so the minimum is attained.

rows.title: Completeness conjecture for regular Inverse Treblecross positions
rows.record_statement:
Let $R$ be the regular set of board states, let a state have at most one piece, and let $\mathcal{G}$ denote its Sprague–Grundy value. **Completeness conjecture.** The regular set $R$ contains all board states that possess at most one piece and satisfy $\mathcal{G} \le 1$, with exactly four isolated exceptions:

$$
[1 X 1],\quad [1 X 4],\quad [4 X 1],\quad \text{and}\quad [4 X 4].
$$

These four states are described as isolated anomalies, and empirical data indicates that all other sufficiently long states in their residue classes have $\mathcal{G}>1$; the completeness of $R$ beyond the stated exceptions remains unproved.
rows.source: Kai Liang and Muxi Li, “A Weak Solution of Inverse Treblecross”, arXiv:2604.16759 (2026).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture (as printed in version 1 of the source, which the MathDB record follows) holds: among boards of Inverse Treblecross with at most one X, those with Sprague–Grundy value at most 1 are exactly the boards of the regular set R together with [1X1], [1X4], [4X1] and [4X4], and each of these four has value exactly 1 and lies outside R. The source computes the values on R and tabulates small cases; what was missing is that no other board, of any length, has value at most 1. Mixed-residue cases are settled in two moves from the source's values for empty boards. When both gaps lie in the critical residue classes, a move at distance four supplies the missing option once the values of an auxiliary family of two-piece boards are known, and those are certified by a coupled induction: a finite abstract-interpretation certificate (each gap known exactly when small, otherwise by its residue modulo 10) checked for all gap lengths at once. Lean defines the game literally on lists of Booleans (a move fills an empty cell without creating three adjacent X's; the value is the mex of the option values), proves the certificate checker sound, proves that the certificate covers every concrete gap length, and proves the classification.

rows.title: Locating chromatic numbers of Cartesian products with cycles and paths
rows.record_statement:
Let $K_m$ be the complete graph, and let $C_n$ and $P_n$ denote the cycle and path on $n$ vertices, respectively. Write $\square$ for the Cartesian product and $\chi_L$ for the locating chromatic number. **Locating chromatic number conjecture for products with cycles and paths.** If $m$ and $n$ are sufficiently large, then

$$
\chi_L(K_m\square C_n)=\chi_L(K_m\square P_n).
$$

The conjecture is motivated by the similarity between the structures of $K_m\square C_n$ and $K_m\square P_n$; no resolution is supplied in the source.
rows.source: Ali Behtoei and Behnaz Omoomi, “On the Locating Chromatic Number of the Cartesian Product of Graphs”, arXiv:1106.3453 (2012).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds with explicit thresholds: for all m ≥ 7 and n ≥ 4 the locating chromatic numbers of K_m □ C_n and K_m □ P_n are equal, both being m + 1 when n ≤ m + 1 and m + 2 otherwise. The path value is Behtoei and Omoomi's own Theorem 2 (re-proved here); the new part is the cycle. Lower bound: each copy of K_m uses m distinct colours, and counting runs of copies that miss the same colour shows that m + 1 colours cannot locate once there are more than m + 1 copies. Upper bounds: for n ≤ m + 1 a cyclic colouring in which each copy misses a different colour, completed by a Hall-type filling; for n ≥ m + 2 two singleton colour classes whose distances separate the copies, with a correction when the cycle is odd. Lean defines the products, graph distance, locating colourings (proper colourings in which the vectors of distances to the colour classes are pairwise distinct) and the locating chromatic number as a least number of colours that is proved to be attained, and proves both formulas and the conjecture.

rows.title: Equidistribution conjecture for type parity at fixed Frobenius number
rows.record_statement:
Let $F(S)$ be the Frobenius number of a numerical semigroup $S$, let $t(S)$ be its type, and let the denominator count all numerical semigroups with Frobenius number $F$. **Frobenius type-parity equidistribution conjecture.**

$$
\lim_{F\to\infty}\frac{\#\{S\mid F(S)=F,\ t(S)\equiv F\pmod{2}\}}{\#\{S\mid F(S)=F\}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The conjecture is motivated by the same numerical data for $F\leq 30$ and predicts asymptotic equidistribution of the two type parities relative to the parity of $F$.
rows.source: Deepesh Singhal, “Numerical Semigroups of small and large type”, arXiv:2008.08110 (2020).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds: among numerical semigroups with Frobenius number F, the proportion whose type has the same parity as F tends to 1/2 as F grows, along all F. Almost all such semigroups have multiplicity close to F/2 (Backelin 1990; the one-sided form needed is proved here). For those, adding or removing the single element ⌊3F/4⌋ gives another numerical semigroup with the same Frobenius number, and the toggle changes the parity of the type unless the semigroup has pseudo-Frobenius numbers at one of a few small gaps from that element; a greedy count of disjoint pairs shows that the exceptional semigroups form a vanishing fraction. So the semigroups pair up, outside a negligible set, into pairs of opposite type parity. Lean defines numerical semigroups as cofinite additive submonoids of ℕ containing 0, the Frobenius number, the pseudo-Frobenius numbers and the type, and proves that the ratio of cardinalities tends to 1/2, both for the sets themselves and for a finite encoding used in the proof.
